The Rasāʾil contain more than one example of this advanced scientific tendency: the recognition that quantitative changes can have qualitative effects. One example appears in al-Risāla al-Jāmiʿa, vol. 1, p. 301, where the Brethren list the contents of the third treatise on the soul. Among other things, it discusses “the mothers of generated beings from which all existing things—minerals, plants, and animals—come into being, and how some change into others as their qualities differ, the numerical amounts of their quantities change, and their structures vary...” We should pay close attention to the phrase “change...as their qualities and numerical quantities differ.” Here “change” means transformation: a transformation in the qualities of beings, indeed “all existing things,” as the passage itself says.↩︎

In the laws of Marxist materialist dialectics, the unity and mutual relationship of quantity and quality is revealed as a principle of change. This is the revolutionary side of the Brethren of Purity’s thought.↩︎

One example comes directly after the passage quoted in the main text: “There is another benefit as well: whenever people know events before they happen, they can ward them off before they occur through prayer and supplication to God...” Even these words point in the same direction: the Brethren reject a fatalistic and deterministic meaning of “necessity.”↩︎

The fact that Arab encyclopedists of this period grasped the law of necessity, even in an early form, confirms the Marxist thesis that practical necessity drives human beings toward knowledge—in other words, their basic material needs. This differs from pre-Marxist philosophies, which explained the drive to knowledge through wonder and amazement at nature. If Arab scientists of the tenth century understood this law, it was because they were connected with the movement of social reality and with the developing production of material necessities. From this they learned how society could protect itself against some of the necessities imposed by natural laws.↩︎

For examples of this progress, see, among others, the English Orientalist Rom Landau, Islam and the Arabs, Beirut, 1962, trans. Munīr al-Baʿlabakkī, pp. 245–249 on mathematics and pp. 258–281 on the natural sciences, chemistry, and medicine.↩︎

In the treatise on “Definitions and Descriptions,” where the Brethren define the technical terms used in the Rasāʾil, they define an “existent” as “that which one of the senses finds, or the intellect conceives, or evidence points to.” See the tenth treatise of the section on psychology and intellect, Rasāʾil, vol. 3, p. 35. This definition might seem to deny the objective existence of the world, because it defines what “exists” in terms of how it is known: through sensation, intellectual conception, or evidence. That would mean either that the Brethren fell into a contradiction or that they did not mean what we have taken the definition to mean. But two points resolve the difficulty. First, the textual evidence supporting our conclusion is explicit. Second, the definition itself says “that which one of the senses finds.” This wording suggests that the “existent” exists objectively before knowledge and that the three ways of knowing merely reveal its existence rather than creating it.↩︎

We should say here that natural science remained unable to explain the world through nature itself until the second half of the eighteenth century. This is why Engels, in the introduction to Dialectics of Nature, complains about the inability of scientists even at this relatively advanced stage, despite the large body of knowledge they had accumulated. He says that science was still deeply immersed in theology and searched everywhere for a “first principle,” only to find it in an external impulse that could not be explained from nature itself. Russian ed.↩︎

One example of what we can now call an absolute truth is the physical proposition that all forms of motion can be transformed into one another. Many ages passed between the first human discovery of the seed of this proposition as a relative truth and its later scientific form. Human beings first discovered that rubbing two pieces of wood together could produce fire. Much later, this discovery was expressed theoretically as the claim that friction, a form of mechanical motion, can be transformed into heat. On this basis, and with the later development of technology, science eventually arrived at the general law that all forms of the motion of matter can transform into one another—an absolute truth. The same applies to all human knowledge whose correctness has been established through scientific experiment.↩︎

By Aristotle’s contradiction here, we mean that he speaks of an unmoved First Mover while also affirming the eternity of motion. These claims appear to conflict. An unmoved First Mover means a mover that is fixed and motionless and is not preceded by motion. But if motion is eternal, then motion precedes it. How, then, can motion be eternal while the First Mover is not preceded by motion?↩︎

(*) Aristotle’s problem arose from his view that the whole universe is a chain of moving things and movers, while a mover must itself be moving in order to move something else. He found no solution to this endless chain except to posit an “intellectual necessity” for a First Mover that does not move, with no temporal gap between it and motion. —Publisher.
